nature-clim-045.title: The adaptation finance gap: needs ten times the money
nature-clim-045.text: Between 2017 and 2021, international public finance to developing countries for adaptation stayed well below US$30 billion per year. The adaptation finance gap is the difference between the estimated cost of adapting and the money available for it. A 2023 study of 85 countries' plans put developing countries' needs at US$387 billion a year up to 2030. On 2017–2021 data, needs are around 10-18 times current public flows, and the gap has widened since earlier assessments. Several things could help close it: more public and private finance, remittances, the money migrants send home, and reform of how vulnerable countries' debts are managed.

nature-clim-046.title: The climate finance gap: hard to measure, easy to inflate
nature-clim-046.text: The climate finance gap is the shortfall between the climate investment needed and what is actually provided. Its size depends on who is counting. Estimates vary with the places, sectors, timescale, target and assumptions used. The reported side is shaky too. Research finds bilateral climate finance, money passed from one country to another, well below official figures. Part of the reason is that there is no agreed definition of international climate finance and no oversight. That has let non-climate projects be counted and raised doubts about official reporting.

nature-clim-049.title: Debt-for-climate swaps: turning repayments into projects
nature-clim-049.text: Seychelles redirected $27 million of debt to marine parks, ocean conservation and ecotourism. A debt-for-climate swap works this way. A country's debt is repaid on new, discounted terms, and the repayments, in local currency, go to domestic climate projects instead of foreign lenders. Projects can include carbon sequestration, renewable energy and protecting biodiversity and oceans. In one Argentine swap, $38,100,000 of debt was addressed and $3,100,000 went to biodiversity, forest and other climate work. The Seychelles deal was a similar debt-for-nature swap.

nature-clim-047.title: Multilateral climate funds: pooled money from many governments
nature-clim-047.text: Multilateral climate funds are governed by several national governments together and pay out money for climate action. As of 2022 the UN climate convention coordinated five. They were {{ref:nature-clim-051}}, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund, the Special Climate Change Fund and the Global Environment Facility. The World Bank coordinates the Climate Investment Funds, active since 2008, made up of the Clean Technology Fund and the Strategic Climate Fund. Some funds give only grants. Others also use cheap loans, equity and risk tools meant to draw in other finance. In 2016 the four main multilateral climate funds approved $2.78 billion of project support.

nature-clim-051.title: The Green Climate Fund: the largest pot, and its quarrels
nature-clim-051.text: Based in Songdo, South Korea, the Green Climate Fund is considered the world's largest fund of its kind. It was set up under {{ref:nature-clim-053}} to help developing countries with mitigation and adaptation. It is the largest of the five {{ref:nature-clim-047}} the convention coordinates. It was named in the 2009 {{ref:nature-clim-061}}, formally established at the 2010 Cancun conference, and its governing instrument was adopted in Durban in 2011. A 24-member board and a secretariat run it. As of November 2026 its portfolio was over $22.3 billion USD, or over $87.1 billion USD including co-financing from other investors. Its Private Sector Facility is among its most controversial features. Many rich countries want it to attract large institutional investors. Developing countries and NGOs want pro-poor finance for small firms. In March 2015 its board refused an explicit ban on fossil fuel projects, effectively allowing coal plants to be funded.

nature-clim-048.title: Private climate finance: why public money is not enough
nature-clim-048.text: Banks, pension funds, insurers, asset managers, companies and households all invest in climate projects. That is private climate finance. Public budgets are often too small for large infrastructure projects, especially in lower-income countries, so private money is seen as needed to fill the shortfall. But climate-friendly projects can cost more up front and carry more risk than fossil-fuel ones, so they must be bankable, able to attract lenders. Over 90% of private climate flows are estimated to stay within national borders. The IMF and OECD warn that private capital alone cannot close the gap. Many adaptation and innovation projects bring high social benefits but low private returns.

nature-clim-095.title: The Kigali Amendment: tackling the ozone fix that warms
nature-clim-095.text: HFCs replaced CFCs and do not harm the ozone layer. But they are greenhouse gases with a high global warming potential. In 2016, the Kigali Amendment to {{ref:nature-clim-094}} committed countries to cut their use of these hydrofluorocarbons by more than 80% over 30 years. It came into force on 1 January 2019. The stakes are large. A 2009 study calculated that a fast HFC phasedown could avoid up to 8.8 Gt CO2-eq per year of emissions by 2050.

nature-clim-096.title: The Montreal Protocol's Multilateral Fund
nature-clim-096.text: The Multilateral Fund helps developing countries with low use of ozone-depleting substances comply with {{ref:nature-clim-094}}. It serves countries using less than 0.3 kg of such substances per person a year; 147 of the 196 parties qualify. It embodies the principle that all share the duty to protect the global commons, but not equally. An executive committee with equal numbers of industrialised and developing countries runs it. It was the first treaty fund managed democratically in this way.

nature-clim-078.title: Climate clubs: fixing free-riding by excluding outsiders
nature-clim-078.text: Why cut emissions if other countries will not? Climate clubs answer the {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. A climate club is a voluntary coalition of countries that agree on a common climate standard, such as a carbon price, and penalise non-members. Membership is voluntary and excludable, so not every country must agree. Countries join for the shared benefit of lower global emissions and to escape sanctions, such as tariffs, imposed on outsiders. The economist {{ref:nature-hist-050}} pioneered the idea in 2015: members price carbon and charge a fee on imports from countries without similar pricing. A 2025 Econometrica paper found such a club could achieve 33–68% of the globally optimal carbon reduction. The G7 Climate Club, launched in December 2022, favours partnerships over penalties and had 46 member states as of May 2025. Opinion is divided. Exporting countries fearing fees and researchers sceptical of {{ref:nature-pol-239}} have criticised it, while others argue supposed losers such as China and India would gain. The EU's CBAM has been called a possible first climate club.

nature-clim-052.title: Additionality of climate finance: is the money really new
nature-clim-052.text: Climate finance given to developing countries is supposed to be new money, additional to existing development aid. The Cancun agreements require this, including for money through {{ref:nature-clim-051}}. New means pledges should come on top of those made in earlier years. But there is no strict definition of additionality. The same vagueness has already caused problems, and even fraud, in judging emission reductions under {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}.

nature-clim-082.title: Climate reparations: compensation as a moral debt
nature-clim-082.text: A 2023 study estimated that the top 21 fossil fuel companies will owe $5.4 trillion in cumulative reparations over 2025–2050. Climate reparations are requested loss-and-damage payments, framed as compensation owed for historical emissions, possibly including debt cancellation. Unlike plain {{ref:nature-clim-018}}, the term treats payment as an ethical and moral obligation. Proposed channels include an international compensation commission, lawsuits, the polluter pays principle, debt forgiveness and direct grants. The wealthiest nations have consistently opposed reparations at the UN climate talks, and some argue current generations are not responsible for past emissions. Before COP27, talks were steered to 'cooperation and facilitation' rather than liability.

nature-clim-091.title: Green banks: public money that draws in private investors
nature-clim-091.text: A green bank is a usually public or quasi-public lender that works with private investors to speed the spread of clean energy technologies. It targets technologies that are commercially viable but slow to spread. It uses public funds to lever in private investment, lowering investors' risk with tools such as cheap loans, guarantees, co-investment and bundling loans for resale. Its public capital can be reinvested again and again across many projects. The US Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 allotted $27 billion to green banks through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund.

nature-clim-101.title: The Bali Action Plan: a road map toward Copenhagen
nature-clim-101.text: In December 2007, COP 13 in Bali set a timeline and structure for negotiating a climate framework for after 2012. Developed countries agreed to comparable quantified emission targets. Developing countries agreed to nationally appropriate mitigation actions, supported by technology, finance and capacity building. A new body, the Ad Hoc Working Group on Long-term Cooperative Action, ran these talks through 2008 and 2009 toward Copenhagen. The conference also drew attention to the 20% of global emissions caused by deforestation.

nature-clim-067.title: ITMOs: emission cuts that cross borders
nature-clim-067.text: In January 2024 Thailand and Switzerland reported the first completed trade of its kind. Internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, or ITMOs, are measured emission reductions or removals that one country transfers to another under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. They count toward the buyer's {{ref:nature-clim-071}}. Countries trade them through bilateral or multilateral deals, without the central crediting mechanism. They can be measured in tonnes of CO2-equivalent or other metrics, and can come from crediting projects or linked emissions trading systems. By 2024 over 80 bilateral agreements were in place. Commentators disagree on whether the transfers mainly cut costs or risk over-crediting and {{ref:nature-clim-058}}.

nature-clim-070.title: Corresponding adjustments: counting each cut once
nature-clim-070.text: If one country sells an emission cut to another, both cannot claim it. A corresponding adjustment is the accounting step that makes sure a transferred reduction counts in only one country's pledge. It guards against double counting, which covers double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit. Countries must report what they authorise, transfer, acquire, cancel or use, and how this appears in their accounts. Registries recording issuance, transfer, cancellation and use make the tracking possible.

nature-clim-069.title: Non-market approaches: cooperation without trading
nature-clim-069.text: Not all cooperation under the Paris Agreement involves trading emission cuts. Under Article 6.8, countries can cooperate voluntarily with no international transfer of reductions at all. These non-market approaches can combine mitigation and adaptation and involve finance, technology transfer and capacity building. A work programme and the Glasgow Committee on Non-market Approaches were set up at COP26 in 2021, and the committee began work in 2022.

nature-clim-068.title: The Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism: UN-supervised credits
nature-clim-068.text: Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement set up a UN-supervised scheme that registers emission-cutting activities and issues credits for verified reductions or removals. Its credits are called A6.4ERs and are tracked in a registry with unique identifiers. Activities are validated, registered, monitored and independently verified before units are issued, overseen by the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body. Two features aim beyond simple offsetting. A share of proceeds goes to {{ref:nature-clim-031}}. A portion of units is cancelled to deliver an overall cut in global emissions.

nature-clim-088.title: The global climate regime: the rules of the game
nature-clim-088.text: The global climate regime is the worldwide framework of rules for regulating how human activity affects the climate, in order to limit climate change. The UN climate convention set its framework, and its first legally binding result was {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. Between 2013 and 2015 there was no legally binding global regime, and the voluntary pledges of {{ref:nature-clim-061}} served in practice. The 2015 Paris Agreement then became the regime. All countries signed on to balancing greenhouse gas sources and sinks in the second half of the century.

nature-clim-099.title: Soft loans: borrowing below the market rate
nature-clim-099.text: A soft loan carries an {{ref:nature-econ-757}} below the market rate. It may also offer other concessions, such as long repayment periods or interest holidays. Governments usually give soft loans to projects they consider worthwhile. The World Bank and other development institutions give them to developing countries. Some official development assistance is counted as the concessional value of soft loans, the gift hidden in their cheap terms.

nature-clim-085.title: Contraction and Convergence: equal shares per person
nature-clim-085.text: Contraction and Convergence is a proposed framework with two moves. Total greenhouse gas emissions shrink to a safe level, and every country's emissions per person converge on the same level. The Global Commons Institute conceived it in the early 1990s and expressed it as a simple mathematical formula. Entitlements start from current emissions and move toward equal shares per person at a negotiated rate. That rate is called a key equity lever. Earlier convergence gives more entitlements to low-emitting, typically poorer, countries. Critics say a per-person basis could reward countries whose populations grow, so the model lets negotiators fix a population base year.

nature-clim-097.title: The ICJ climate opinion: a court weighs in
nature-clim-097.text: Pacific island students drove it, and Vanuatu led the request. On 29 March 2023 the UN General Assembly asked the International Court of Justice what international law requires states to do to protect the climate. The Court answered on 26 July 2025. It unanimously held that the climate treaties create binding obligations, including submitting national pledges and acting on {{ref:nature-clim-084}}. Breaching them is an internationally wrongful act that can require full reparation, given a clear causal link. Any state may invoke another's breach, because the climate is a global common good. The opinion is not binding but is expected to be used in courts.

nature-clim-102.title: The New Collective Quantified Goal: from $100 billion to $300 billion
nature-clim-102.text: In 2009, developed countries set a goal, agreed at Cancún in 2010, to mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries. They missed it in 2020 and reached it only in 2022. An OECD report gave $132.8 billion in 2023 and $136.7 billion in 2024. The New Collective Quantified Goal is its successor, negotiated at COP29 in 2024 to cover support after 2025. In Baku, delegations agreed that developed nations would pledge $300 billion a year by 2035, from public and private sources. Poorer nations called this insufficient, and many pushed for at least $500 billion. Some critics, including UN officials, called it a betrayal. The donor base was a key tension. The US and EU wanted countries such as China and the Gulf states to contribute, but the text only encouraged voluntary contributions. Talks at COP30 were expected to address scaling finance from $300 billion to $1.3 trillion.

nature-clim-092.title: A short history of climate policy
nature-clim-092.text: Formal global environmental politics began in June 1972, with the UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm. The first World Climate Conference, in 1979, framed climate change as a global political issue. The IPCC followed in 1988. Most efforts since have sought consensus at the UN under its climate convention, with the 1987 Montreal Protocol cited as proof this can work. Critics of that top-down approach propose bottom-up governance instead. Adaptation was long seen as a distraction from mitigation. It gained attention only around 2009 and 2010, after the Copenhagen summit made progress on emissions look harder. Climate policy also became increasingly polarised in the late 2000s. By 2020 the US partisan gap was the widest in history.

nature-clim-090.title: The first global stocktake: a verdict delivered in Dubai
nature-clim-090.text: On 13 December 2023, COP 28 in Dubai concluded the first {{ref:nature-clim-089}}, part of the UAE Consensus. Its verdict was blunt. A 43 percent emissions cut by 2030 was needed, but only a 5 percent cut was expected. It set 2030 targets to triple renewable energy capacity and double global energy efficiency. For the first time at a UN climate conference, it called on all countries to transition away from fossil fuels to reach climate neutrality by 2050. It also set up the loss and damage fund, with $700 million in start-up capital, to be run by the World Bank.

nature-clim-081.title: Adaptation debt: paying for harm others caused
nature-clim-081.text: Poorer nations suffer the worst consequences of a problem they did little to cause. Adaptation debt is the compensation developing countries claim they are owed for climate damage caused by the developed world's emissions. The burden compounds. Lacking infrastructure and capital, poor countries often borrow at higher interest to recover from disasters, worsening their prospects. The UN climate convention notes that the debt can be met through financial aid and help coping with natural disasters.

nature-clim-080.title: Emissions debt: overusing the atmosphere
nature-clim-080.text: Since around 1750 the United States alone has produced 25% of all carbon emissions, and developed countries together 70%. Emissions debt is the part of {{ref:nature-clim-079}} owed for that imbalance. The atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions is called the total carbon space. The claim is that rich countries used more than their fair share of it. Repayment would mean helping poorer countries industrialise cleanly and sharing out the remaining carbon space by population.

nature-clim-057.title: Too weak or too strong: the case against Kyoto
nature-clim-057.text: Critics attacked {{ref:nature-clim-056}} from opposite sides. Some environmentalists and scientists found its commitments too weak, while several economists thought them stronger than justified. Stavins called it 'too little, too fast'. Stern said its lack of a long-term goal kept it from sending a credible signal. Others objected that it set cuts only for rich countries and none for fast-growing economies such as China and India. Nordhaus argued that its limits on quantities were less efficient than setting a price, and that it might be better redesigned as a global carbon tax.

nature-clim-062.title: The Cancún agreements: pledges and a new fund
nature-clim-062.text: At the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún, 76 developed and developing countries made voluntary mitigation pledges. Together they produced 85% of global annual emissions in 2010. Parties agreed that future warming should stay below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. Developed countries committed to jointly mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries, and created {{ref:nature-clim-051}}. That finance had to be 'new' and 'additional' to existing aid.

nature-clim-061.title: The Copenhagen Accord: a deal the conference only noted
nature-clim-061.text: The 2009 Copenhagen conference had been seen as the chance to agree a successor to {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. Instead a group of countries produced the Copenhagen Accord, which the conference only 'took note of'. It said warming should be limited to below 2.0 °C, which the UN climate secretariat reads as relative to pre-industrial temperatures. In all, 114 countries agreed to it. Seventeen developed parties plus the EU-27, and 45 developing parties, submitted mitigation targets. It set the goal of sending $100 billion a year to developing countries by 2020 and proposed the Green Climate Fund.
